articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. on October 27, 2026. This settlement resolves apparent violations of OFAC sanctions programs.

Details of the violations and the terms of the settlement were not immediately released in the initial announcement, but such agreements typically involve a monetary penalty and commitments from the company to enhance its compliance protocols.
This action underscores OFAC's continued focus on enforcing sanctions compliance across various industries and highlights the importance for companies to maintain robust internal controls.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting Requirements
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026, providing updated guidance on blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

These amendments aim to clarify existing regulations and assist financial institutions and other entities in complying with their sanctions obligations. The updated FAQs often address common compliance challenges and provide practical interpretations of OFAC's rules.
The issuance of amended FAQs is a regular practice by OFAC to ensure that its guidance remains current and responsive to evolving sanctions landscapes and industry inquiries.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, Issues New General Licenses
body: On October 21, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related designations, alongside removals of designations related to Belarus and North Korea. The action also included the issuance of new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations are part of ongoing efforts to counter illicit activities supporting the Iranian regime. Concurrently, the removals for Belarus and North Korea suggest a recalibration of sanctions policy in those areas.
The new General Licenses and amended FAQs provide crucial guidance for navigating the updated sanctions landscape, particularly concerning permissible transactions with Iran and Russia.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.
PAIPA targets individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property, aiming to safeguard U.S. economic interests and national security.

The accompanying General Licenses are intended to mitigate any unintended consequences of these designations, providing clarity on permissible activities and ensuring that legitimate transactions are not unduly disrupted.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question. This update provides further clarification and potential adjustments to existing sanctions against Venezuela.
The amendment likely addresses specific types of transactions or activities, reflecting ongoing policy considerations regarding the humanitarian situation or diplomatic efforts in Venezuela.
Such amendments are crucial for entities engaging with Venezuela, as they define the scope of permissible activities under the complex sanctions regime.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Iran-Related and Cuba Designations, Issues General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related and Cuba designations on October 15, 2026. These actions are accompanied by the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations are part of the ongoing 'Operation Economic Outcast' aimed at financially isolating the Iranian regime, targeting sectors such as digital assets, technology, gold, aviation, and shipping.

The Cuba designation and related guidance reflect the continued implementation of Executive Order 14404, which imposes sanctions on those responsible for repression in Cuba and threats to U.S. national security.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action signifies a potential shift in U.S. policy towards certain individuals or entities associated with Venezuela.

The delisting of Jorge Rodriguez, President of Venezuela's National Assembly, from OFAC's Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) list, ends an asset freeze and removes obstacles for U.S. persons to deal with him.
This removal comes amid broader U.S. efforts to engage in diplomacy and expand energy investment in Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Targets
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations on October 13, 2026. These designations target individuals and entities involved in illicit drug trafficking and terrorist financing networks.
These actions are part of ongoing efforts to disrupt the financial infrastructure of criminal organizations and terrorist groups, aiming to protect the U.S. financial system from abuse.
The designations underscore the U.S. government's commitment to combating transnational crime and terrorism through financial sanctions.

articles.headline: Bank of America Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Bank of America, N.A. on October 13, 2026. The settlement addresses apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs.
The settlement amount for OFAC violations was $11,662,930, part of a larger enforcement action that also included penalties from FinCEN and the OCC.

This action highlights the critical importance for large financial institutions to maintain robust sanctions compliance programs to prevent violations across multiple regimes, including those targeting Iran, Russia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Settles with OFAC; ICC and Burma Designations Updated
body: On October 9, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. This action was coupled with new designations related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated General Licenses, as well as a Burma-related designation removal.
The settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics addresses apparent violations of OFAC sanctions regulations, underscoring the agency's enforcement efforts in the logistics sector.
The ICC designations and accompanying General Licenses reflect U.S. policy regarding the court, while the Burma-related removal indicates a specific adjustment to sanctions targeting that country.

articles.headline: EU Adopts 22nd Sanctions Package Against Russia, Targeting Military-Industrial Complex
body: On October 12, 2026, the European Union adopted its 22nd package of sanctions against Russia, marking the largest single expansion of its sanctions listings since 2022.

The new measures add 1,569 individuals and entities to the EU sanctions lists, comprising 826 Russian companies and 743 individuals. These designations primarily target Russia's military-industrial complex, including businesses involved in the production and supply of components for missiles, drones, and military aircraft.

The package also includes sanctions against 77 political figures connected with the September 2026 elections held in occupied Ukrainian territories. This action reinforces the EU's commitment to increasing pressure on Russia in response to its ongoing aggression against Ukraine.
articles.source: Council of the EU / Squire Patton Boggs

articles.headline: EU Sanctions Three Individuals and Four Entities Over DPRK Nuclear and Missile Programs, Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union adopted additional restrictive measures on October 12, 2026, against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations target those responsible for supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities contributing to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings specifically address activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

articles.headline: EU Renews Sanctions Regime Against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda Until 2027
body: The Council of the European Union renewed its autonomous restrictive measures against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda and associated persons, groups, undertakings, and entities on October 26, 2026.

The sanctions regime has been prolonged for another year, until October 31, 2027. The autonomous list currently includes 15 persons and 8 groups, all subject to an asset freeze and, for individuals, a travel ban to the EU.
These measures complement those imposed by the UN Security Council and underscore the EU's continued commitment to countering the terrorist threat posed by these organizations.

articles.headline: UN Security Council Renews Haiti Sanctions Regime for One Year
body: The UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2831 (2026) on October 14, 2026, renewing the sanctions regime concerning Haiti for another year.
The renewed measures include a travel ban, asset freeze, and arms embargo, aimed at addressing the ongoing gang violence and instability in the Caribbean nation.

The resolution was adopted with 14 votes in favor and one abstention from the Russian Federation, highlighting international concern over the misappropriation of public resources and illicit financing that sustain criminal groups in Haiti.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

articles.headline: UN Security Council Committee Amends Three Entries on ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List
body: On October 26, 2026, the Security Council Committee pursuant to resolutions 1267 (1999), 1989 (2011), and 2253 (2015) concerning ISIL (Da'esh), Al-Qaida, and associated individuals, groups, undertakings, and entities enacted amendments to three entries on its ISIL (Da'esh) and Al-Qaida Sanctions List.
These amendments involve specific updates to the listed individuals and entities subject to the assets freeze, travel ban, and arms embargo.
Such adjustments to the UN Consolidated List are routine and reflect ongoing efforts to maintain the accuracy and effectiveness of international sanctions regimes against terrorist organizations.
articles.source: UN Meetings Coverage and Press Releases

body: American consumer confidence saw a rebound in October, driven in part by a modest decline in gasoline prices, although energy costs remain elevated.

The Conference Board Consumer Confidence Index increased by 7.5 points to 91.7 in October, reflecting a more positive outlook on price stability. Despite this, average 12-month inflation expectations among consumers, while declining, remained elevated at 5.8%.

This recovery in consumer sentiment provides a mixed signal for the U.S. economic outlook, with some economists noting that while current financial circumstances appear stable, concerns about future economic conditions persist.

body: Cuba has accused the United States of threatening countries with tariffs, visa restrictions, and other retaliatory measures to influence their votes on an upcoming United Nations resolution calling for an end to the long-standing U.S. embargo against the island.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez stated that U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and U.S. Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz are personally leading this campaign, which he described as a 'new and dangerous way of conducting multilateral diplomacy.'

The UN General Assembly has historically voted overwhelmingly in favor of non-binding resolutions seeking to end the U.S. economic embargo, which has been in place for over six decades and is credited with exacerbating economic hardship in Cuba.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions for October 2026, Including Penalties Against Major Banks
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, including significant penalties against major financial institutions.

American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah, received a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence violations.

Bank of America, National Association, Charlotte, North Carolina, was assessed a $750 million civil money penalty for similar deficiencies in its BSA compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

articles.headline: OCC Issues Prohibition Orders Against Former Bank Employees for Embezzlement
body: As part of its October 2026 enforcement actions, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) issued Orders of Prohibition against two former bank employees for embezzling customer funds.
Jennifer Hamblin, a Vault Teller at a Cincinnati, Ohio, branch of Fifth Third Bank, N.A., was prohibited for embezzling approximately $292,000.

Christopher Organista, a Former Operations Processor at the La Mirada, California Operations Center of U.S. Bank National Association, was prohibited for embezzling approximately $194,131 in bank customer funds.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah (bank), for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA Violations
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) announced a $1.2 billion penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for its failure to mitigate and report priority national security risks, including Chinese money laundering networks and illicit finance along the southwest border.

As part of its resolution with FinCEN, Bank of America admitted to willfully violating the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) by failing to implement and maintain an adequate Anti-Money Laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence for correspondent accounts for foreign financial institutions, and file Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs).

The consent order found that the bank's deficient internal controls and proprietary transaction monitoring system resulted in missed and delayed detection and reporting of over $5 billion in suspicious activity, with approximately $1 billion implicating national security-related risks.

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
